lesson.title: Rest, Digest, Restore: The Parasympathetic Nervous System
lesson.summary: This section explains the parasympathetic nervous system, the branch of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and restores energy once a threat has passed, and how it balances the sympathetic response covered previously.
lesson.body:
The parasympathetic nervous system is the second of the two branches of the autonomic nervous system, and it functions as the natural counterbalance to the sympathetic nervous system covered in the previous section. Where the sympathetic branch mobilizes the body for fight or flight in response to threat or stress, the parasympathetic branch does essentially the opposite job, calming the body back down and supporting the quieter, restorative processes that keep the body functioning well over the long run. This function is often summarized with the phrase rest and digest, a deliberate contrast to fight or flight.

The physiological changes produced by the parasympathetic nervous system largely mirror the sympathetic changes described earlier, only in reverse. Heart rate slows back down. Pupils constrict rather than dilate. Digestion, which the sympathetic system had suppressed, resumes and is actively promoted, along with salivation. Breathing slows and deepens. Essentially, wherever the sympathetic nervous system revved a particular process up in preparation for action, the parasympathetic nervous system winds that same process back down once action is no longer needed, returning the body toward its resting baseline.

The relationship between these two systems is best understood as a balance rather than a simple on and off switch. Continuing the earlier analogy, if the sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, the parasympathetic nervous system is the brake, and a well functioning nervous system shifts fluidly between the two depending on what a given moment actually calls for. A healthy stress response is not the absence of sympathetic activation, since some sympathetic activation is appropriate and adaptive when a real challenge appears, but rather the ability to also engage the parasympathetic system afterward and return to baseline once the challenge has passed, rather than remaining stuck in a heightened state indefinitely.

Returning to the hiker from the previous section's example makes the parasympathetic system concrete. Once the hiker gets a closer look and realizes the coiled shape on the trail is only a fallen stick, not a snake, their body does not stay keyed up forever. Within a few minutes, the parasympathetic nervous system takes over: heart rate drops back down, tense muscles relax, and breathing slows back to its normal, resting rhythm, restoring the hiker to the same calm baseline they were at before rounding the bend in the trail.

Stepping back, these final sections trace one connected story: a central nervous system that makes decisions, a peripheral nervous system that links it to the rest of the body, a somatic branch for voluntary movement and an autonomic branch for involuntary regulation, and within that autonomic branch, two opposing forces, sympathetic and parasympathetic, working together to let the body shift automatically between mobilization and recovery exactly as each moment demands.
